title: “Mind or machine?”: Study protocol for a mixed-methods study evaluating the effectiveness and lived experience of active versus passive prophylaxis in older hip fracture patients
content:
by Haowei Du, Xin Chen, Minghui Wang, Xiangyu Piao, Huisong Liu

Background

Hip fracture in older adults causes a “dual crisis” of venous thromboembolism (VTE) and rapid muscle atrophy. Pharmacological prevention is effective but carries significant bleeding risks for these frail patients. Current physical prophylaxis is often too weak to restore muscle pump function. Therefore, this study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of two enhanced strategies, active resistance training and passive neuromuscular electrical stimulation, against standard care for VTE prevention and muscle preservation.

Methods

A three-arm, assessor-blinded, parallel-group RCT will be conducted at a tertiary hospital in Qingdao, China. Older patients (n = 222) recovering from hip fracture fixation will be randomized in a 1:1:1 ratio to: (1) the control group; (2) the control plus lower-limb resistance training group; or (3) the control plus neuromuscular electrical stimulation group. The primary outcome is the incidence of ultrasound-confirmed VTE within the intervention period. Secondary outcomes include venous hemodynamics, muscle architecture, self-reported fatigue, and cost-effectiveness. Quantitative data will be analyzed using intention-to-treat principles. Following the RCT, a qualitative interpretive phenomenological analysis study will be conducted with a purposive sample of 10–12 participants to explore the lived experiences, barriers, and facilitators associated with adhering to “active” versus “passive” rehabilitation models.

Discussion

This study addresses the lack of data comparing active versus passive therapies for hip fracture patients. Active training promotes voluntary muscle use, potentially boosting patient confidence. In contrast, electrical stimulation guarantees muscle pumping regardless of fatigue. If effective, this study will validate a new “dual protection” strategy. This will help establish an optimal rehabilitation model to solve the “dual crisis” of thrombosis and muscle loss.

Trial registration

The study was pre-registered at the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry on March 17, 2026. Trial Registration Number: ChiCTR2600120624.
